title: Thermodynamic-kinetic and dilatometric characterization of the influence of Mo and Cu additions on phase transition behavior in high-strength medium-Mn steels
abstract: Abstract Theoretical and experimental critical temperatures as well as phase transition phenomena during continuous cooling in 4 mass. % Mn advanced steels with and without Mo and Cu additions were investigated in the present study. The thermodynamic–kinetic calculations were performed using JMatPro software and phase transformations were recorded using a DIL805 dilatometer. The research covered slow austenitization and continuous cooling rates from 60 to 0.05 °C s −1 . The issues related to both modelling and dilatometric methodology were discussed. All analyzed steels exhibited very high hardenability as at a cooling rate of 1 °C s −1  all microstructures were martensitic. Only decreasing the cooling rate to 0.05 °C s −1  resulted in the formation of full bainitic microstructure in a base material and partly bainitic–martensitic microstructure in an alloy enriched by 0.3 mass.% Mo. The steel with the addition of 0.3 mass.% Mo and 1 mass.% Cu exhibited fully martensitic microstructure even after cooling at 0.05 °C s −1  indicating the strong effect of both Mo and Cu on steel’s hardenability increase. The obtained microstructures were very homogeneous and ultrafine.
journal: Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Modern steels used for advanced forgings require the combination of high strength and fracture toughness/resistance under static, dynamic and cyclic loading conditions. Moreover, they need to be easy machined and excellent hardenability is required to guarantee stable microstructures and mechanical properties throughout the whole forging [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5 ]. Up to now, there are no steel processing concepts available that effectively combine the above-mentioned mechanical properties at an acceptable production cost. The most widely used concepts are quenching and tempering (Q&T) and precipitation hardening ferritic–pearlitic (PHFP) steels that provide only a part of the properties specified above.

The application of advanced multiphase steels containing retained austenite (RA) is a response to the current requirements of the automotive industry in Europe and around the world. The presence of metastable austenite enables the simultaneous increase in strength and ductility of multiphase steels [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]. These types of steel contain Si and Al additions, which inhibit the formation of carbides. Hence, carbon is allowed to enrich within the remaining austenite leading to a decrease of its martensite start temperature (M s ) below room temperature, i.e., stabilizing the RA [ 7 ]. The production of ultrafine-grained microstructures containing RA opens new avenues of steel processing leading to an outstanding combination of strength and ductility [ 9 ]. The grain refinement also increases both the fatigue strength and the fracture toughness [ 10 ,  11 ]. Initial works in this field have been carried out for multiphase steels containing RA. However, the research is limited to conventional multiphase steels (with Mn contents below 2%). Sugimoto et al. [ 12 ] investigated the effect of thermomechanical processing on mechanical properties of medium-C steel containing: 0.42% C, 1.51% Mn, 1.47% Si, 0.50% Cr, 0.20% Mo, 0.48% Al and 0.052% Nb. The produced multiphase steel revealed a microstructure composed of small amounts of polygonal ferrite, bainitic ferrite and RA in the form of blocky grains and films located between laths of bainitic ferrite. Samples obtained by isothermal holding at 350 °C for 1000 s were characterized by a good combination of high strength and fracture resistance. Specimens produced under such conditions reveal the following properties: yield strength (YS) ~ 880 MPa, ultimate tensile strength (UTS) ~ 1390 MPa and KV − 80 J. The main drawbacks of these steels are difficult machinability (due to a high C content) and non-homogeneous microstructures due to the presence of polygonal ferrite and blocky-type RA. Some research [ 13 ] was carried out on steels with a microstructure composed of bainite and RA. In this case, forging was followed by controlled cooling to 350 °C-450 °C and isothermal holding for a few minutes. These steels were characterized by YS in a range from 700 to 1000 MPa and KV − 100–120 J. Microalloying of Ti or Nb has a beneficial effect on the toughness due to the reduction in the size of bainitic laths. A similar processing schedule was applied for a steel containing 0.24% C, 0.70% Si, 1.58% Mn, 0.80% Cr and Ti, V and B microaddition [ 10 ]. After austenitizing at 1150 °C, the steel was forged and then cooled to 375, 400 and 425 °C, where it was held until the transformation was completed. After such treatment, the samples showed microstructures composed of bainitic ferrite and 15% RA.

Nowadays, one of the most promising group of steels for future forging applications are medium-manganese steels with fine-dispersed RA. Usually, these steels contain 3–10% Mn, 0.2–0.3% C, 0.5–1.5% Si/Al and some addition of Nb, Ti, Mo or B microalloying. Due to the presence of ductile RA located between the martensite, bainitic ferrite or ferrite laths, an advantageous combination of strength, ductility and fatigue strength could be expected. Mechanical properties of these steels are related to the cooling rate applied after hot forging and/or depend on parameters of subsequent heat treatment [ 14 ,  15 ]. An additional advantage of these steels should be their increased impact toughness resulting from the reduced C content. The presence of filmy RA significantly improves the ductility and fracture toughness. The RA prevents crack initiation by (i) accommodating local plasticity and (ii) blocking propagating microcracks due to the martensite formed as a result of plastic deformation [ 11 ,  16 ].

Quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels are in great demand as potential candidates for third generation of advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) [ 17 ]. This type of heat treatment has been started in cold-rolled low-alloy transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) sheet steels containing 0.2–0.5% C, 1–1.5% Mn and 1.5% Si in order to obtain high-strength martensitic microstructures with RA [ 18 ]. However, this approach has not been yet applied for forging designs. Q&P steels show ultra high strength levels (YS > 1100 MPa, UTS > 1400 MPa), KV ~ 20–40 J and TEl > 10%. Increasing the Mn content to 4–5% should contribute to further increasing the hardenability and strength. The type of heat treatment was first presented by Speer et al. [ 19 ]. The Q&P heat treatment sequence consists of reheating the steel to the intercritical annealing (IA) temperature or full austenitization, quenching to a temperature between M s  and M f , and then heating to a higher temperature for C and eventual Mn partitioning [ 20 ]. Martensite is formed during the initial quenching step, and the final martensitic–austenitic mixture is obtained. The purpose of this heat treatment is to stabilize the RA by the diffusion of carbon from supersaturated martensitic laths into the RA phase. As the austenite is enriched in carbon, its M s  temperature is lowered; once the M s  temperature falls below room temperature (RT), all austenite present in the microstructure is retained at RT [ 21 ]. Cooling rate to quenching and its temperature are the crucial parameters influencing mechanical properties of these steels. The quenching rate controls the decomposition of austenite and the quenching temperature governs the amount of initial martensite, and therefore the volume fraction of RA in the microstructure [ 22 ]. Both of these parameters are directly controlled by the chemical composition of the alloy. Therefore, thermal characterization of the given alloy undergoing Q&P treatment is essential in order to correctly determine critical temperatures and design the heat treatment.

Another issue to be solved in the steel industry is the increasing share of residual elements from the recycling of steel scrap [ 23 ]. Cu is one of the contaminant elements that accumulate in steels during repeated recycling. It enters postconsumer steel scrap through brass, bronze, coatings, plating, cables, and engine parts from electrical gadgets and vehicle scrap, as well as electrical and electronic waste [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. In high-performance sheet steels (particularly applies to sheet steels for forming operations), Cu is not used as an alloying element, but instead is an impurity [ 26 ,  27 ]. Due to the expected continuous increase in the concentration of this element in "green" steel, it is necessary to determine its influence on the thermal characteristics of steel as it may severely change critical temperatures and the kinetics of phase transformation.

The current research aims to perform a detailed thermodynamic–kinetic analysis of medium-Mn alloys intended for forging with some variations in Mo and Cu concentrations, which is a response to the current situation on the automotive green steel market. The knowledge of critical temperatures and phase transition behavior are crucial in designing multi–step thermal cycles needed in advanced multiphase QP steels.

sections.heading: Material and methods
paragraphs: The alloying concept is partially based on previous work [ 28 ] and was modified to achieve the above-described goals. Thermodynamic–kinetic calculations for designing the chemical compositions as well as thermal analysis were conducted using the JMatPro (General Steels Module v11.2 database) software. The chemical composition simulations concerned the influence of Mo and Cu on alloy’s phase composition, equilibrium diagrams and phase transformation kinetics during cooling. The final chemical composition of new designed melts using thermodynamic calculations is presented in Table  1 . Table 1 Chemical composition of produced medium-Mn alloys Chemical element/mass.% C Mn Si Al Mo Cu Base 0.18 4.00 0.52 0.76 – 0.3 Mo 0.17 4.02 0.51 0.75 0.3 – 0.3 Mo 1 Cu 0.17 4.10 0.52 0.79 0.3 1.04

The carbon content was selected to be lower than 0.2 mass.% to improve machinability of forgings. A relatively low manganese content was selected to enable production of at least 10% of RA during Q&P process and to limit technological problems related to this element, like microsegregation [ 29 ,  30 ], hydrogen embrittlement [ 31 ], hole expansion ratio [ 32 ,  33 ] or increased hot working resistance [ 34 ]. Si and Al were added to prevent or delay carbides’ precipitation. The second alloy was enriched by 0.3 Mo to increase its hardenability [ 35 ] and ensure possibility of air cooling after austenitization without triggering ferritic, pearlitic or bainitic transformations. The third alloy was additionally enriched by about 1% Cu to simulate the steel produced from recycled steel scrap [ 36 ,  37 ]. Based on the alloy design three, laboratory melts with a mass of approximately 80 kg were produced in a vacuum induction furnace. The melts were cast into ingots with a 140 × 140 mm 2  cross section and cooled to room temperature. For homogenization, the ingots were consecutively submitted to thermomechanical treatment, consisting of homogenization at 1250 °C for 5 h, followed by hot forging to a final cross section of 60 × 60 mm 2 . After the forging, the samples were air-cooled to RT. The obtained bars were used for further experiments. Experimental investigations of the effect of different heat treatments were performed using a BÄHR high-resolution DIL805A/D. Cylindrical dilatometric samples with a diameter of 5 mm and a length of 10 mm were machined from the forged material along the transverse direction. The dilatometric investigations were performed in a vacuum atmosphere; helium gas was used for cooling. The specimen temperature was measured using a S-type thermocouple welded to the central part of the length of the sample. During the experiments, the fused silica push rods were used. First, heating and cooling thermal cycles were performed to determine A c1 , A c3 , M s  and M f  temperatures of the alloys and to investigate the influence of cooling rate on phase transformation kinetics. In order to approach equilibrium conditions the initial heating rate of 200 °C/h was selected based on the work [ 38 ]. The cooling was performed at 60, 1 and 0.05 °C s −1  to investigate the alloy’s hardenability and occurring phase transformation. The dilatometric data were analyzed according to ASTM A1033-04 standard [ 39 ]. The beginning of the phase transitions was determined as the point where the dilatation curve deviates from the straight line [ 40 ,  41 – 42 ]. The theoretical and experimental results were compared.

After the dilatometric tests, samples were sectioned in half of the lengths, embedded in the thermosetting resin, grinded using SiC paper with grid up to 2000, and polished using diamond paste of 3 μm and 1 μm particle sizes. Therefore, the microscopic observations were performed along the axis of the transverse direction—the rolling direction was observed. For microstructural observations by light microscope the samples were etched using 3% nital for − 4 s at room temperature. The microstructure of steel was investigated using a Zeiss Observer Z1m light microscope. The hardness of the heat treated samples was measured using a Future-Tech FM-700 Vickers hardness tester at a load of 1 kgf. Twelve measurements for each sample were taken. The extreme values were discarded and the average value of the remaining measurements was calculated.

sections.heading: Design of chemical composition
paragraphs: Conventional alloying elements of medium-Mn steels are: C, which affects solid solution strengthening and partly controls the austenite stability [ 43 ,  44 ]; Mn, whose major role is to increase the austenite stability, but additionally it increases alloy’s hardenability [ 45 ]; and Si and Al, which are mainly added to prevent and/or inhibit the precipitation process of carbides to enrich the remaining part of austenite in carbon [ 46 ]. The results of their influence may be found elsewhere [ 47 ,  48 ]. In this study, the base steel is composed of these four alloying elements, which are in a range to ensure good machinability, strength, ductility and a desired RA fraction after the Q&P process of at least 10%. Since the aim of this work is to analyze the effect of Mo and Cu additions on thermal characteristics of steel, the research was started by simulating the effect of different additions on the critical temperatures of the equilibrium state (Fig.  1 ). The theoretical A 1  and A 3  temperatures of base material are 589 and 830 °C, respectively (Fig.  1 a). At lower temperatures, the carbides of the type M 23 C 6 , M 7 C 3  and cementite are present (Fig.  1 b). The results indicate that even a relatively high addition of Mo reaching 0.4 mass.% does not significantly affect the phase equilibrium of the analyzed steel (Fig.  1 a). The A 1  and A 3  temperatures for the Mo alloyed steel are higher only by 4 °C. In the case of carbides, two new types appear, which are M 6 C and M 2 (CN); however, their total fractions are at similar levels. A slightly more noticeable difference occurs in the case of Cu alloyed steel (Fig.  1 c,d). The addition of 2 mass. % Cu decreases the A 1  and A 3  temperatures by 5 and 16 °C (Fig.  1 c) as it is an austenite stabilizer [ 49 ]. In the case of carbides, no relevant difference is visible (Fig.  1 d) in comparison with the base material. After lowering the temperature below 785 °C the metallic Cu can be precipitated with a phase fraction of ~ 2% at RT. Fig. 1 Simulated equilibrium diagrams for analyzed steels with different additions of Mo  a ,  b  and Cu  c ,  d ; F—ferrite, A—austenite

The thermodynamic–kinetic simulations on the influence of cooling rate on phase transformation are presented in Fig.  2 . Results indicate that an increase in Mo concentration in steel increases its hardenability significantly, which is in agreement with the literature [ 50 ]. Based on the calculations, the addition of only 0.1 mass. % Mo decreases the critical cooling rate for ferrite from 8 °C s −1  to 0.9 °C s −1  (Fig.  2 a). In case of the bainitic transformation, the difference is 10 and 4 °C s −1 , respectively. The changes in Mo concentration do not affect M s  and M f  temperatures of the alloy. In case of Cu, an increase in hardenability is also identified since the addition of 2 mass.% Cu decreases the critical cooling rate for ferritic transformation from 8 to 1 °C s −1  (Fig.  2 b). Also the M s  temperature decreases along the increasing addition of Cu (305 °C for the base material and 291 °C for the steel with 2 mass.% Cu). A similar tendency was observed in the literature [ 49 ]. In regard to bainite formation, the simulations suggest that the Cu addition does not influence the bainitic transformation kinetics, which contradicts previous results for standard quench and tempering steels [ 51 ]. Fig. 2 Simulated influence of cooling rate on the phase transformation kinetics for alloys with different Mo  a  and Cu  b  concentrations

The Mo addition to the steel at a level of 0.3 mass.% was chosen to increase its hardenability and improve the hot ductility of medium-Mn alloys [ 52 ]. Its content should be as low as possible to enable the technological and economic production of steel since it is an expensive and has a comparably high environmental impact [ 53 ]. The Cu addition was selected to represent a worst-case scenario of the residual concentration in current and future green steel produced from recycled scrap [ 23 ,  37 ]. The thermodynamic and thermodynamic–kinetic simulations of selected alloys are presented in Fig.  3 . They indicate that a slight decrease in both A 1  and A 3  temperatures should be expected for Cu alloyed steel. The M s  temperature should be lower in Mo and Mo + Cu alloyed steels, which enables to produce martensite with a higher dislocation density [ 54 ]. The critical temperatures are summarized in Table  2 . In paper [ 55 ] the authors obtained 12 and 90 °C reduction of A 1  and A 3 , respectively, by the addition of 1.5 mass.% of Cu and Ni. In work [ 56 ], 1.22 mass.% of Cu caused a decrease in A 1  and A 3  temperatures reaching 11 and 24 °C, respectively. A decrease in M s  temperature resulting from an increase in austenite stability was also observed. sections.heading: Verification of thermodynamic-kinetic simulations
paragraphs: The dilatometry (Fig.  5 ) confirms tendencies identified by thermodynamic-kinetic calculations, but the absolute values of A c1 , A c3 , M s  and M f  temperatures differ significantly with variations from 40 to 60 °C in all cases (Table  2 ). Works [ 59 ,  60 ] indicate that these differences may be explained by the inaccuracy of currently available models in the software used. The diffusion kinetics are not included at this stage of the model development and need to be addressed in future works because manganese gradients in austenite may be present due to slow diffusion coefficient of Mn, especially in austenite [ 61 ]. Despite the significant differences in results, we believe that the use of thermodynamic calculations is useful as it provides guidance and outlines the path to achieving the intended goals. The A c1  and A c3  for the base alloy are 652 and 897 °C, respectively (Fig.  5 a,b). The addition of 0.3 Mo mass.% increases these temperatures only by 1 and 7 °C, respectively, which confirms the tendency suggested by simulations. Further addition of 1 Cu mass. % decreases the A c1  and A c3  temperatures by 9 and 20 °C in comparison with the Mo alloyed steel and 5 and 16 °C in comparison with the base steel. The M s  and M f  temperatures for the base and Mo alloyed steels are very similar (0 °C difference in case of M s  temperature and 16 °C in case of M f  temperature). The addition of Cu increases significantly the austenite stability since the M s  temperature is lower by 17 °C and M f  temperature by 19 °C. Fig. 5 Experimental dilatometric results of selected alloys registered at slow heating of 200 °C/h  a ,  b  and quenching at 60 °C s −1 c ,  d  allowing for determination of the critical temperatures

Next, dilatometric investigations concerning different cooling rates (1 and 0.05 °C) from the austenitization temperature of 1000 °C were performed and compared to the simulation results (Fig.  6 ). It is indicated that at a cooling rate of 1 °C s −1  the base alloy should be fully composed of bainite, while Mo and Cu alloyed steels should be composed of a mixture of martensite and bainite (Fig.  6 a). The dilatometric results (Fig.  6 b) indicate that in case of all three alloys, the occurring transformations are very similar and take place in a temperature range characteristic for martensitic transformation (350–150 °C). At a cooling rate of 0.05 °C s −1 , the simulations indicate the formation of ferrite and pearlite in the base sample, and mostly pearlite in Mo and Cu alloyed samples (Fig.  6 c). The experimental dilatometric curves obtained at a cooling rate of 0.05 °C s −1  are similar to those obtained with 1 °C s −1  (Fig.  6 a). In case of the base alloy, an intense transformation starting at about 450 °C is identified, which can be initially assigned to the bainitic transformation. In case of the 0.3 Mo alloy, the intense transformation starting at − 410 °C is visible and followed by a second subtle transformation starting below 350 °C, as magnified in Fig.  6 e. The first transformation may be again assigned as bainitic, whereas the second one may be martensitic. In case of the 0.3 Mo 1 Cu steel, the single transformation takes place in the temperature range characteristic for martensitic transformation for this alloy. These observations and interpretations have been confirmed by microscopic observations and hardness tests (Fig.  7 ). Fig. 6 Comparison of simulated  a ,  c  and experimental  b ,  d ,  e  results for the kinetics of phase transformations occurring during cooling at different rates (1 and 0.05 °C s −1 ) for selected alloys; M—martensite, B—bainite, P—pearlite, F—ferrite Fig. 7 Microstructures  a – i  and hardness results  j  for samples after cooling at different rates; M—martensite, B—bainite

The microstructure after quenching performed at 60 °C s −1  reveals martensitic microstructures for all alloys (Fig.  7 a–c) and similar hardness levels (Fig.  7 j) to the initial material (Fig.  4 d). After lowering the cooling rate to 1 °C s −1 , the microstructures are still martensitic (Fig.  7 d–f) as indicated by dilatometry (Fig.  6 b). The hardness is similar or slightly lower (12 HV1 for Mo alloys and 16 for Mo Cu alloys), which may be caused by self-tempering of martensite due to slow cooling (Fig.  7 j). This is supported already by optical microstructure as the martensite laths seem to be decorated with very small particles. However, detailed electron microscopy is necessary to fully reveal the nature of these features. From that, air cooling after austenitization/hot working/heat treatment can be applied because the tested cooling rate of 1 °C s −1  is lower than the average cooling rate obtained with air cooling [ 62 ,  63 ]. Only at cooling rates smaller than 0.05 °C s −1 , which results roughly in 5.5 h of cooling, the base material has a fully bainitic microstructure, which is also represented by a 67 HV1 drop in hardness to the value of 353 HV1 (in comparison with the quenched steel). In case of the steel with 0.3 mass.% Mo addition, the dominant phase is bainite but some martensitic regions are distinguished as well. The hardness for this sample is 78 HV1 lower in comparison with the quenched one. Only the Mo + Cu alloyed steel exhibits fully martensitic transformation despite very slow cooling from the austenitization temperature. Its hardness is also lower than for the quenched one but only by 26 HV1 (Fig.  7 j), which indicates the strong effect of Cu on self-tempering kinetics, which will be analyzed in future works. The high hardenability of analyzed steel is a significant advantage of the material in terms of its industrial production. It allows to obtain comparable results regardless of the cooling mode used on the production line.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The investigations addressed the thermodynamic-kinetic simulation and experimental verification of phase transitions in 0.18C-3Mn-0.5Si-75Al medium-Mn alloy designed for advanced forgings and its variations with 0.3 Mo, and 0.3 Mo + 1 Cu. It was found that: The thermodynamic-kinetic simulations and experimental dilatometric results show similar tendency; however, the specific critical temperatures of the alloys are significantly different (at least 40 °C) due to the inaccuracy of currently available models for novel chemical composition designs including increased Mn and Al contents. The Mo addition has a minor influence on the A c1 , A c3 , M s  and M f  temperatures of the alloy. Mo affects significantly the hardenability of the steel as the calculated 0.3 mass.% addition decreased the critical cooling temperature from 10 to 4 °C s −1 . Its addition increases the hardness of the alloy by − 20 HV1 and − 10 HV1, respectively at the cooling rates inducing martensitic and bainitic microstructures. The 1 mass. % Cu addition has more significant influence on the A c1  (decrease by 9 °C), A c3  (decrease by 20 °C), M s  (decrease by 11 °C) and M f  (decrease by 10 °C) temperatures of the alloy in comparison with the Mo alloy. Cu affects significantly the hardenability of the steel. The steel with 0.3 mas.% Mo and 1 mass.% Cu exhibits fully martensitic microstructure even after cooling at a rate of 0.05 °C s −1 , whereas the base material exhibits fully bainitic microstructure under such conditions. Cu + Mo addition increases the hardness of the alloy by ~ 50 HV1 regardless of the cooling rate. The high hardenability of all produced alloys enables applying air cooling after their austenitization, hot-working or heat treatment because the cooling rate of 1 °C allows to obtain fully martensitic microstructure, and is comparable to air cooling conditions. The produced medium-Mn steel is characterized by ultrafine microstructure regardless of the additions of Mo and Cu
